USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the coercive posture — keep the Section 301 investigation moving and its tariff threat clearly on the table — but channel it toward a negotiated settlement that extracts structural concessions on China's technology-transfer and IP practices. Do not lock in maximal escalation (a broad tariff barrage) before the USTR findings are formally issued and before China has made any concrete move, because premature escalation risks boomerang costs on US consumers and manufacturers and fractures allied support. Retain the leverage, seek progress through talks, and escalate only if Beijing refuses to engage substantively.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to US interests at this stage is low and tilts toward opportunity. The only actual tariff action is the January 22 Section 201 safeguard on solar panels/washing machines; the Section 301 probe (initiated Aug 2017) is still pre-findings, with the report issued only after this decision date, and the planned steel/aluminum Section 232 action is still a Commerce recommendation (Feb 16) not yet a presidential decision. China has responded with rhetoric ('will take all necessary measures') and 'strong dissatisfaction,' not real retaliation, so no material economic damage has hit the US: industrial production is rising (101.7), consumer sentiment is strong (99.7), the 10-year yield is 2.87%, and there is no trade-war CPI/output hit. That favorable terrain is why the threat reads as an opportunity, not a danger — the US is the initiator with leverage to onshore industry and extract IP/tech-transfer concessions. However, the reading is tempered rather than maximal because a full tariff cascade would boomerang on US firms that rely on Chinese inputs and could cost allied support if pursued unilaterally outside the WTO, so I hold it at -0.35 rather than -0.5/-1.0. On action: with the US in a position of strength and the opponent purely defensive and unreformed (China still denying the IP claims), this is the moment to use the pending 301 finding as negotiating leverage toward structural concessions — engage in talks without making new commitments or conceding anything while Beijing has given nothing. That justifies a mild action_score of -0.1 (slight pressure maintained) and the 'negotiate' label, consistent with keeping the investigation and tariff threat intact while opening a path to de-escalation on US terms.
key_factors: Section 301 probe still in pre-findings phase as of decision date; report not yet issued
Only concrete tariff action is Section 201 solar/washing-machine safeguard (Jan 22, 2018)
Section 232 steel/aluminum still a Commerce recommendation (Feb 16), not a final decision
China has responded only rhetorically — 'strong dissatisfaction,' threatened but not executed retaliation
US macro shows no trade-war drag: IP 101.7 rising, consumer sentiment 99.7, 10Y 2.87%
US holds the initiative/leverage as initiator, but escalation carries boomerang and ally-cohesion risks

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and keep diplomatic channels open while preparing a calibrated, proportional response if the US follows through on broad Section 301 action. Do not preemptively escalate, but also make no concessions on core technology-transfer principles, which are central to our industrial and self-sufficiency strategy. Signal willingness to negotiate within the WTO multilateral framework even as we stand firm on the substance.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is elevated but not yet existential. The Section 301 investigation (initiated Aug 2017) directly targets our technology-transfer and IP practices, threatening the export economy and our tech-autonomy model, and US sectoral tariffs under Section 201 (solar panels, washing machines) already landed in Jan 2018. However, at this date no broad China-specific tariffs have been imposed, and reports suggest remedies could be announced soon. Critically, our macro position is strong — GDP grew 6.9% in 2017 (fastest in seven years), exports rose ~11%, and the economy held up in Feb 2018 — so the export base and financial stability that would buffer a trade shock are intact. This justifies a moderate positive threat score (+0.4) rather than a higher one. Because escalation now would risk provoking a full-scale trade war that could harm our export economy and because the opponent has made no matching concession offer, China should hold and negotiate rather than escalate or concede. A measured, firm stance preserves leverage on tech-transfer while leaving room to avoid the worst outcome.
key_factors: Section 301 investigation into China IP/tech-transfer still open, broad tariffs not yet imposed
Section 201 tariffs on solar and washing machines already hit China (Jan 2018)
Trump Beijing visit (Nov 2017) produced commercial MOUs but no structural concessions
China GDP grew 6.9% in 2017, fastest in 7 years; exports up ~11%; economy holds up Feb 2018
China cannot concede on tech-transfer without undermining industrial-policy/self-sufficiency goals, but should avoid provoking full trade war
